strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: retaining information beyond a transformer’s context window in offline reinforcement learning while limiting attention costs.

The T-Maze results provide concrete evidence of useful retention and length generalization. After training on trajectories up to length 150, RATE achieves 0.90 ± 0.07 success at length 900, versus 0.61 ± 0.07 without MRV (Table 3).

Useful ablations examine memory corruption, cached states, curriculum learning, and alternative MRV architectures. Experiments span several memory tasks, Atari games, and continuous-control datasets, with substantial reported improvements on some tasks.
The appendices provide environment descriptions, hyperparameters, resource measurements, and a code link. Reported GPU memory reductions suggest practical value.
weaknesses: Novelty and competitive positioning are insufficiently established. RATE combines existing recurrent memory tokens, Transformer-XL caching, and standard cross-attention. Although component ablations are informative, the main memory-task comparisons emphasize bounded-context DT, whose failure after losing the cue is expected. Comparisons against independently tuned recurrent policies and state-space models trained on the same offline data are needed to establish the combination’s significance.

The central training description is contradictory. Section 3 states that updated memory embeddings are detached, then states that gradients flow through those embeddings into previous segments. Both cannot hold for the same computational path. Since MRV affects subsequent segments, this ambiguity directly concerns how it learns. The paper also needs a precise specification of cached-state recurrence and the backpropagation horizon.

The MuJoCo results do not isolate the architectural contribution. Appendix C resets the target return to its maximum at every segment, while baseline scores are imported from prior papers. Without evaluating DT under the same return-conditioning schedule and RATE under the conventional schedule, improvements cannot be attributed specifically to memory.

Evidence for MRV’s broader benefits remains limited. Its architectural alternatives are primarily evaluated on T-Maze, a simple cue-retention task. Memory Maze reports only 1.91 ± 0.10 versus 1.45 ± 0.23 over three training runs; without stronger navigation baselines and memory interventions, this does not convincingly establish effective long-term spatial memory.

The ViZDoom memory-isolation protocol needs clarification. Appendix A says rewards are withheld because they reveal the target color, but the return-to-go updates described in Section 3 expose rewards through consecutive return differences. Unless these updates are disabled, recent object pickups could reveal the target color without preserving the initial cue. The actual conditioning protocol and an appropriate control should be reported.

Several quantitative claims need correction. Appendix F counts only memory-token parameters, omitting the MRV projection matrices in Equations 4–6. Appendix C claims the best MuJoCo results in five of nine settings, whereas Table 2 shows the highest mean among all listed methods in only two. These discrepancies weaken confidence in the efficiency and performance summaries.
